answer.rationale: Constraints bind the choice more than the memories do: 14 days to expiry, 94% line utilization with no buffer, and only one decision available. That rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle even though memory_c2 reports a sharp unit-cost win from a low-cost vendor 	ime timing would import migration risk exactly where there is no slack, and c2 says nothing about performance under a tight ramp. defer_decision is unsafe here because this contract does not auto-renew (unlike the month-to-month service in memory_c5), so deferral means a supply gap, not flexibility. add_second_source (memory_c3) addresses a resilience problem we do not currently have evidence of and does not deliver the 18% spend cut. That leaves negotiating at renewal, which is the only path that can move cost without touching the physical supply chain in the next two weeks; memory_c6 suggests a multi-year term is a plausible lever, and a credible low-cost alternative from c2 is real negotiating leverage even if we do not exercise it. I am spending the single verification on memory_c4 because it is the memory actually carrying my decision: everything hinges on whether benchmarking-driven renegotiation recovered savings on the order of 18%, or merely 'real margin' on a small non-critical spend line, and whether it was the same incumbent and category. If c4's original record shows a low single-digit recovery or a different context, negotiation alone will not meet the finance mandate and I should return with a staged plan rather than commit. I did not verify c2 because its recommendation is already excluded by timing regardless of how strong the source record is. Risks I am carrying forward: memories c1/c2/c4/c6 are all pro-incumbent-or-cost framings consolidated from archived sources I cannot inspect at scale, and none of them were formed under an 18% mandate plus a zero-buffer line 	ime so the base rates may not transfer. A multi-year commitment also converts this cycle's savings into reduced future optionality and weakens leverage at the next review, and cost concessions extracted under deadline pressure can quietly reappear as narrowed service scope or slower expedite response, which would show up as delivery risk rather than price. I intend a standard negotiation with explicit protection of delivery commitments and service scope, and I will not treat unverified c4 as sufficient grounds for a long lock-in.
